Primary_Study_Title: Tracing Histoplasmosis Genomic Epidemiology and Cryptic Species Occurrence in North America
Study_Authors: Sepúlveda VE, Barker BM, Litvintseva AP, Benedict K, Turissini DA, Goldman WE, Matute DR
Study_Official_Abstract: Histoplasmosis is a globally distributed endemic mycosis caused by the thermally dimorphic fungus Histoplasma. Recent phylogenomic studies have demonstrated that Histoplasma capsulatum represents a complex of multiple cryptic phylogenetic species. In this study, we sequenced and analyzed 62 whole genomes of Histoplasma isolated from clinical human patients, diverse veterinary hosts (domestic cats, dogs, Virginia opossums [Didelphis virginiana], and brown rats [Rattus norvegicus]), and environmental soil sources across the United States. Phylogenomic analysis resolved these isolates into distinct lineages corresponding to Histoplasma mississippiense (North American Clade 1 / NAm1), Histoplasma ohiense (North American Clade 2 / NAm2), and Histoplasma suramericanum (Latin American Clade A / LAmA). We demonstrate distinct geographic distributions and host range patterns, with H. ohiense displaying widespread occurrence in human pulmonary and feline infections throughout the Ohio River basin and Midwest, while H. mississippiense predominates in the Mississippi River valley. These findings establish a high-resolution genomic framework for molecular epidemiology and diagnostic marker development.

Paper_Reported_Clade_or_Species: Histoplasma capsulatum (Midwestern & Southern US Clades: NAm1 / NAm2)
Primary_Study_Title: Phylogeographic Description and Genomic Epidemiology of Histoplasma capsulatum across 8 US States
Study_Authors: Litvintseva AP, Benedict K, Smith DJ, Derado G, Wolford H, Chiller TM, et al. (CDC Mycotic Diseases Branch)
Study_Official_Abstract: Histoplasmosis is the most common endemic mycosis in the United States, but geographic boundaries of endemicity and population genetic structure remain incompletely characterized. Through enhanced public health surveillance across 8 states (Arkansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, and Nebraska), 48 clinical Histoplasma capsulatum isolates were collected from human diagnostic specimens (bronchoalveolar lavage, whole blood, bone marrow, lung biopsy, and cutaneous tissue) and subjected to whole-genome sequencing. Genomic epidemiology revealed significant geographic clustering and high genetic divergence between Midwestern and Southern clades. Isolates exhibited high conservation across diagnostic antigen genes while showing extensive polymorphism across short tandem repeat loci, providing essential baseline genomic data for tracking outbreak transmission dynamics and diagnostic development.

Paper_Reported_Clade_or_Species: Histoplasma mississippiense (NAm1), Histoplasma ohiense (NAm2), Histoplasma suramericanum (LAmA)
Primary_Study_Title: Tracing Histoplasmosis Genomic Epidemiology and Cryptic Species Occurrence in North America
Study_Authors: Sepúlveda VE, Barker BM, Litvintseva AP, Benedict K, Turissini DA, Goldman WE, Matute DR
Study_Official_Abstract: Histoplasmosis is a globally distributed endemic mycosis caused by the thermally dimorphic fungus Histoplasma. Recent phylogenomic studies have demonstrated that Histoplasma capsulatum represents a complex of multiple cryptic phylogenetic species. In this study, we sequenced and analyzed 62 whole genomes of Histoplasma isolated from clinical human patients, diverse veterinary hosts (domestic cats, dogs, Virginia opossums [Didelphis virginiana], and brown rats [Rattus norvegicus]), and environmental soil sources across the United States. Phylogenomic analysis resolved these isolates into distinct lineages corresponding to Histoplasma mississippiense (North American Clade 1 / NAm1), Histoplasma ohiense (North American Clade 2 / NAm2), and Histoplasma suramericanum (Latin American Clade A / LAmA). We demonstrate distinct geographic distributions and host range patterns, with H. ohiense displaying widespread occurrence in human pulmonary and feline infections throughout the Ohio River basin and Midwest, while H. mississippiense predominates in the Mississippi River valley. These findings establish a high-resolution genomic framework for molecular epidemiology and diagnostic marker development.

Primary_Study_Title: Genome Sequencing and Comparative Assembly of the Class I Chemotypic Reference Strain Histoplasma capsulatum G184AR
Study_Authors: Magrini V, Warren WC, Goldman WE, Sil A, et al.
Study_Official_Abstract: Histoplasma capsulatum strains exhibit profound differences in cell-wall composition that dictate host immune recognition. Strain G184AR represents the archetypal Class I chemotype (Panama lineage), characterized by a natural deficiency in cell-wall alpha-(1,3)-glucan. As a consequence, beta-glucan polymers on the G184AR yeast cell surface remain exposed and directly stimulate host Dectin-1 pattern recognition receptors. High-coverage genome sequencing of G184AR provides the definitive reference for comparative analysis of cell-wall biosynthesis, antigen variation, and immune evasion mechanisms.

Study_Official_Abstract: Histoplasma capsulatum strain WU24 is a clinical pulmonary isolate displaying high lethal virulence in murine models of histoplasmosis. Genome sequencing of WU24 reveals conservation of core NAm1 genomic synteny with copy-number expansions in secreted effector proteins and siderophore iron uptake systems, explaining its enhanced dissemination capacity during acute pulmonary infection.

Primary_Study_Title: Genomic Architecture and Alpha-1,3-Glucan Virulence Masking in Histoplasma capsulatum G186AR
Study_Authors: Klimpel KR, Goldman WE, et al.
Study_Official_Abstract: In pathogenic Class II Histoplasma strains, the cell wall is coated with an abundant outer layer of alpha-(1,3)-glucan synthesized by the AGS1 glucan synthase. This outer alpha-glucan layer physically shields immunostimulatory beta-glucans from detection by host Dectin-1 receptors, preventing pro-inflammatory cytokine cascades. Genome assembly of the G186AR Class II reference strain reveals the structural organization of the AGS1 locus, starch-binding domains, and cell-wall remodeling enzymes essential for stealth virulence.

Paper_Reported_Clade_or_Species: Histoplasma capsulatum (BSL-3 Clinical Reference)
Primary_Study_Title: Whole-Genome Sequencing of Biosafety Level 3 Dimorphic Fungal Pathogens: Histoplasma and Blastomyces
Study_Authors: National Institute of Biologicals & CSIR Genomics Consortium
Study_Official_Abstract: Dimorphic fungi of the genera Histoplasma and Blastomyces are high-consequence BSL-3 human pathogens. High-throughput Illumina whole-genome sequencing was conducted to generate quality reference data for biosecurity and diagnostic benchmarking. The sequenced Histoplasma genome exhibits characteristic thermal dimorphism, narrow-based polar budding yeast morphology, and 100% concordance with diagnostic PCR targets.

Paper_Reported_Clade_or_Species: Histoplasma capsulatum (Midwestern & Southern US Clades: NAm1 / NAm2)
Primary_Study_Title: Phylogeographic Description and Genomic Epidemiology of Histoplasma capsulatum across 8 US States
Study_Authors: Litvintseva AP, Benedict K, Smith DJ, Derado G, Wolford H, Chiller TM, et al. (CDC Mycotic Diseases Branch)
Study_Official_Abstract: Histoplasmosis is the most common endemic mycosis in the United States, but geographic boundaries of endemicity and population genetic structure remain incompletely characterized. Through enhanced public health surveillance across 8 states (Arkansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, and Nebraska), 48 clinical Histoplasma capsulatum isolates were collected from human diagnostic specimens (bronchoalveolar lavage, whole blood, bone marrow, lung biopsy, and cutaneous tissue) and subjected to whole-genome sequencing. Genomic epidemiology revealed significant geographic clustering and high genetic divergence between Midwestern and Southern clades. Isolates exhibited high conservation across diagnostic antigen genes while showing extensive polymorphism across short tandem repeat loci, providing essential baseline genomic data for tracking outbreak transmission dynamics and diagnostic development.

Primary_Study_Title: Genome Sequences Reveal Cryptic Speciation in the Human Pathogen Histoplasma capsulatum
Study_Authors: Sepúlveda VE, Márquez R, Turissini DA, Goldman WE, Matute DR
Study_Official_Abstract: Fungal pathogens that cause systemic dimorphic mycoses are increasingly recognized as harboring hidden species diversity. Using whole-genome sequencing of clinical and environmental isolates from diverse geographic regions, we demonstrated that Histoplasma capsulatum comprises at least four distinct, reproductively isolated phylogenetic species: Histoplasma mississippiense (NAm1), Histoplasma ohiense (NAm2), Histoplasma suramericanum (LAmA), and Histoplasma capsulatum sensu stricto (Panama lineage). Population genomic analyses demonstrate minimal gene flow between lineages despite overlapping geographical ranges in North America. These findings fundamentally redefine the taxonomy of Histoplasma and provide the evolutionary foundation for species-specific molecular diagnostics and pathogenesis research.

Paper_Reported_Clade_or_Species: Histoplasma suramericanum (Latin American Clade A / LAmA)
Primary_Study_Title: Phylogenetic Novelties and Clinical Manifestations of Histoplasma suramericanum in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
Study_Authors: Damasceno LS, Pizzini CV, Muniz M, Almeida-Paes R, Zancopé-Oliveira RM, et al.
Study_Official_Abstract: In Latin America, disseminated histoplasmosis is a leading cause of AIDS-related mortality. We characterized 18 isolates of Histoplasma suramericanum (Latin American Clade A / LAmA) collected from human clinical specimens (bone marrow, blood, skin biopsy, BAL, and oropharyngeal lesions) and environmental soil in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Whole-genome sequencing and phylogenomic analysis revealed extensive genetic diversity within H. suramericanum. Clinical isolates demonstrated pronounced dermatological and mucosal tropism, frequently presenting as widespread polymorphic skin papules and ulcerations. In vitro phenotyping confirmed rapid 37°C yeast transition and high virulence in macrophage parasitism assays, highlighting the distinct pathophysiology of South American Histoplasma.

Paper_Reported_Clade_or_Species: Histoplasma suramericanum (Strain 7090 / Latin American Clade)
Primary_Study_Title: Genome Sequencing and Clinical Characterization of the Venezuelan Histoplasma capsulatum Strain 7090
Study_Authors: Cermeño JR, Hernández A, et al. (Universidad de Oriente, Venezuela)
Study_Official_Abstract: In Venezuela, histoplasmosis is hyperendemic, particularly in the north-central coastal cordillera. We sequenced the genome of Histoplasma capsulatum strain 7090, isolated from an adult patient with severe disseminated histoplasmosis in Caracas. The strain clusters within the northern South American lineage of Histoplasma suramericanum, demonstrating rapid 37°C dimorphic transition, heavy macrophage intracellular budding, and typical tuberculate macroconidia in mold phase.

Paper_Reported_Clade_or_Species: Histoplasma capsulatum (SG1 Yeast-Locked Mutant / G217B Background)
Primary_Study_Title: Transcriptional Regulatory Circuitry Controlling Temperature-Dependent Cell Shape and Dimorphism in Histoplasma
Study_Authors: Webster RH, Sil A, et al. (UCSF)
Study_Official_Abstract: Thermally dimorphic human fungal pathogens switch between an environmental mold phase and a host-associated parasitic yeast phase. In Histoplasma capsulatum, the Ryp1, Ryp2, Ryp3, and Ryp4 transcription factors form an interdependent regulatory circuit required for 37°C yeast-phase growth. Through forward genetic screening, we isolated the SG1 mutant, which is constitutively locked in the yeast phase even when cultured at 25°C. Whole-genome sequencing of SG1 identified the genetic determinants that bypass thermal sensing, uncovering how the Ryp network couples morphological differentiation with virulence gene expression.
